name: Olga Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or government, and nothing you say today will be linked to your name. To start, can you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a haul truck at the copper pit outside Bremley, the big one everyone just calls the Hole. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off, and I'm up at four to catch the crew bus on Station Road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the driving itself look like, hour to hour?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: You line up under the shovel, wait for the bucket to drop two hundred-odd tonnes in the tray, and feel the whole cab sink. Then it's the ramp, down to the crusher, tip, back again, maybe thirty loads a shift. I like the quiet up there and I like the people on the radio, but the night shifts in winter wear me right down now. My back tells me I'm fifty-eight every time I climb that ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Half the stuff they put in the lunchroom newsletter about the future of mining is sales talk from people who've never sat in a cab. I'd probably post something like that on the union page too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish my time the way I planned. Seven more years, then the pension kicks in at sixty-five and Samir and I can stop setting alarms. That's all I've wanted for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep paying my union dues, and keep putting the bit we put away each month into the savings account. Maybe I'd finally book the trip to see our daughter Leila in the city without feeling guilty about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a breath out. Not happy exactly, just relieved that the ground isn't moving under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the company newsletter. What do they actually say about AI at the Hole right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've got a trial on the north ramp with three trucks that drive themselves, run from a room in the city. Management calls it the future, and the drivers call it the ghost fleet. Even in this picture I reckon those three stay, they just don't spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the ghost fleet stays at three trucks, does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still be watching them on the ramp and giving them plenty of room, because they stop dead if a rabbit runs across. It's annoying, but annoying I can live with.

S0.say: I'd tell people it was mostly sales talk all along, and that the people writing the newsletters have never sat in a cab. I'd probably post that on the union page too.
S0.think: Privately, it means I get to finish my last seven years the way I planned and take my pension at sixty-five. That's really all I want now.
S0.do: Keeps working her four-on, four-off roster and paying union dues. Keeps putting the same monthly amount into savings and finally books a trip to visit her daughter in the city.
S0.feel: Relieved more than happy. She feels the ground has stopped moving under her.
S0.quote: Management calls it the future, and the drivers call it the ghost fleet.
S0.fieldNote: Olga is calm here because her whole plan rests on seven more ordinary years, and this picture gives her exactly that. She already lives next to a small self-driving trial at her pit and treats it with a weary shrug. Her public and private views are close; the main difference is that privately she cares less about being right and more about the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what the union says: if machines take over the trucks, the company owes us a proper deal, not a handshake and a cake. Online I'd be angrier. I'd say the shareholders get the savings and the town gets the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think haul trucks are exactly the first thing to go. The ghost fleet goes from three trucks to thirty, and someone like me, average driver, never touched a computer if I can help it, is the easy one to let go. I'm not the person they'll pick for the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting, which I'll admit I've been skipping. I'd ask the rep straight out what the redundancy terms are for someone with twenty-two years in, and whether there's a bridge to the pension. We'd stop the extra spending, no new car, and I'd try to get on the water cart or the grader roster, something they'll automate later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'm angry, but under the anger I'm frightened of being sat at home at sixty with nothing to do and less money than we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try for the water cart or the grader. Would you take training for the control room if it were offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say no, and I know how that sounds. I can't stand screens, and I'd be sitting next to twenty-five-year-olds who grew up on games. I'd rather drive something old than be the slow one in a room full of monitors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Samir cut first if the pay looked shaky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new car, straight away; we'd keep the old car going. Then the holiday money. We've got about four months put by, which sounds fine until you remember the mortgage on the block of land we bought for retiring.

S1.say: I'd say the company owes drivers a proper deal if machines take over the trucks, not a handshake and a cake. Online I'd say the shareholders get the savings and the town gets the bill.
S1.think: Privately I think haul trucks go first, and an average driver who avoids computers is the easy one to let go. I don't see myself being picked for the control room.
S1.do: Starts going to every union meeting and asks for the redundancy terms and a bridge to her pension. Drops plans for a new car and the holiday, and tries to move onto the water cart or grader roster that will be automated later.
S1.feel: Angry on top and frightened underneath, mostly of being at home at sixty with less money than planned.
S1.quote: I'd rather drive something old than be the slow one in a room full of monitors.
S1.fieldNote: This mild scenario already lands hard because haul trucks are the most obvious thing at her mine to automate. She'd refuse retraining for the control room, and she knows it sounds stubborn, which she admits openly. Her plan is to hide in the slower corners of the job and lean on the union, and she blames shareholders more than the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud. I'd say this is a choice, not the weather, and the government should make the companies pay into a fund for every driver they take off. I'd be on the picket line if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'm sixty and out of a job five years before the pension. Four months of savings doesn't stretch five years, it doesn't even stretch to Christmas twice. I think it means we sell the block we bought for retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd be in the union office making them fight for a pension bridge, and I'd sign anything that goes to the government. We'd stop every spare dollar, put the block of land up for sale, and I'd ring our son Tariq about the granny flat at his place, just in case. After it arrives I'd try for any cleaning or gate work at the mine, anything with a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. I keep picturing the lunchroom empty and the bus not stopping at Station Road anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years to see it coming change things, compared with a slower version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing in a mining town. With two years I'm just in the queue with everyone else. You can't retrain, you can't sell a house properly, and every other driver at the Hole would be dumping their stuff at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dot, who I eat lunch with, she's fifty-one and on her own with a mortgage. And the young guys who just bought trucks on finance. At least I've got Samir's wage from the school buses, if the buses still have drivers.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that this is a choice, not the weather, and the government should make companies pay into a fund for every driver they take off. I'd join any picket line.
S2.think: Privately I think I'm out of work at sixty, five years before my pension, with savings that won't last. It probably means selling the land we bought to retire on.
S2.do: Goes to the union office in the first month to push for a pension bridge and signs every petition to government. Puts the retirement block up for sale, stops all spare spending and asks her son about his granny flat; after it arrives, applies for cleaning or gate work at the mine.
S2.feel: Sick to her stomach, picturing an empty lunchroom and a crew bus that no longer stops.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing in a mining town. With two years I'm just in the queue with everyone else.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning the gap between her job ending and her pension starting is what alarms her, not AI itself. She immediately reaches for the union, government and family, which fits her outlook. The detail about everyone selling at once in a one-industry town was sharp and unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say it with a plan attached. I'd want the union to start bargaining now, while they still need us, not in year four when the trucks are already here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough to the pension that a decent payout and a bit of retirement savings could carry us across. It's still not what I wanted, but it's a gap I can picture closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to negotiate early-exit terms now, and I'd put my name down for them. We'd put more away each month, maybe an extra few hundred, and pay down the land instead of selling it. I'd also stop saying no to every extra shift while they're still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not sick like the fast one. It's more of a long grumble in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd never take control-room training. With five years, would you think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd go along to the info session, I'll give you that. But I'd still be the slowest in the class, and I'd rather spend those years earning overtime than sweating over a course I'll fail. That's probably stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila and Tariq about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to worry about us, then I'd tell them to make sure their own jobs have a person in them in five years. Tariq's an electrician, so he reckons the robots will need wiring. Leila's nursing, and I'm less sure about anything now.

S3.say: I'd say the union should start bargaining now while the company still needs us, not in year four when the trucks are already here. I'd say it with a plan attached this time.
S3.think: Five years takes me to sixty-three, close enough that a decent payout and my retirement savings might carry us to the pension. It's not what I wanted, but it's a gap I can picture closing.
S3.do: Pushes the union to negotiate early-exit terms now and puts her own name down. Saves a few hundred extra each month, pays down the retirement block instead of selling it, and takes every overtime shift on offer.
S3.feel: Worried in a slow, grumbling way rather than sick. The extra time takes the edge off.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend those years earning overtime than sweating over a course I'll fail.
S3.fieldNote: Five years changes her from defending to bargaining: she wants an early-exit deal while drivers still have some weight at the table. She opens the door to retraining a crack, then closes it again herself. Her plan is to work hard, save and leave early rather than adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a problem for the young ones and we need to look after them, apprentices especially. I'd still post that the companies should share what they save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I've already retired when it lands. I'll be sixty-eight, sitting on the porch, watching it on the news. My worry moves to the kids and to the town, not to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work my seven years as planned and keep paying into my retirement fund. I'd keep going to union meetings, more for the younger members, and I'd vote for whoever promises a fund for mining towns. I'd talk to Tariq about whether he should stay in Bremley at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about me and uneasy about everyone else. It's like knowing a storm's coming after you've already moved house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in the town if the mine ran itself by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pub would close, the football club would struggle, and the school would lose kids. My whole street is mine families. Ten years lets people move away slowly instead of all at once, I suppose, which is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this mostly worries you for others. Is there anything in it that worries you for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My retirement fund's partly in mining shares, which is funny if you think about it. And if Samir loses the bus job early, we'd be down a wage. But no, I'd mostly be out of the road by then.

S4.say: I'd say it's a problem for the young ones and we need to look after apprentices especially. I'd still post that the companies should share what they save.
S4.think: Privately I think I'll be sixty-eight and already retired when it lands. My worry shifts to my kids and the town rather than myself.
S4.do: Works her remaining seven years as planned and keeps paying into her retirement fund. Stays active in the union for younger members, votes for a mining-town fund and talks to her son about whether to stay in Bremley.
S4.feel: Calm about herself, uneasy about the town and her kids.
S4.quote: It's like knowing a storm's coming after you've already moved house.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year version is the one where her age protects her, and she knows it. She moves from fear to a kind of watchful concern for her son, her street and the football club. Her one personal crack is her husband's bus job, which she brushes past.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. What would help is a bridge to the pension for anyone over fifty-five who loses their job to machines, paid for by the companies that make the money. I don't want a course, I want to get to sixty-five with the house still ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. There's only a handful of us drivers, and it took years to get a toilet near the pit. I'd hate for all that fight to end with a robot getting the job we finally got in the door for.

headlineQuote: I don't want a course, I want to get to sixty-five with the house still ours.
portrait: Olga Rahman is a 58-year-old haul truck driver at a big open-pit copper mine outside the town of Bremley, with twenty-two years in and a pension she's counting down to at sixty-five. She avoids computers, distrusts the small self-driving truck trial at her pit, and reaches first for her union and the government when things go wrong. She's calm if AI stalls, anxious under steady change because haul trucks are the obvious first target, and alarmed if AGI lands in two years and leaves her five years short of her pension. With ten years' warning she'd already be retired, so her worry turns to her son, her husband's bus job and her town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose her job at sixty and face a five-year gap before her pension with only about four months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A company-funded bridge to the pension for anyone over fifty-five who loses their job to machines. She'd rather keep her house than be offered a course.
